name: Beresheet 2
short_status: Engineering frozen since April 2025 for lack of funding, and described by SpaceIL as a freeze rather than a cancellation. The follow-up to the crashed Beresheet was designed as one orbiter and two small landers on a single launch, but has no active schedule as of October 2026.
tagline: SpaceIL and Israel Aerospace Industries · Lander · 2020 · Commercial and multipolar In development
stats: spacecraft on one launch: an orbiter and two landers
estimated budget, planned as largely philanthropic
landing sites targeted, including a private far-side first
engineering suspended since Apr 2025, though never cancelled

facts.label: Announcement
facts.value: Unveiled 9 December 2020 by Israeli President Reuven Rivlin as a redesigned three-craft mission (one orbiter and two landers); an initial Beresheet 2 concept had been floated in 2019 after the first lander crashed

facts.label: Builders / operator
facts.value: SpaceIL (Israeli nonprofit) with Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI); Shimon Sarid named CEO in February 2020, alongside SpaceIL co-founder Kfir Damari

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: One orbiter released with two small landers on a single launch; the orbiter would stay in lunar orbit for a multi-year mission (about five years) as a science and education platform while the two landers touched down at separate sites, billed by SpaceIL as the first dual-lander deployment and the smallest landers ever to soft-land on the Moon

facts.label: Far-side ambition
facts.value: The plan called for one lander on the near side and one on the far side; a successful far-side touchdown would make Beresheet 2 the first privately built spacecraft to land on the lunar far side (only China's Chang'e 4 and Chang'e 6 have landed there)

facts.label: Estimated cost
facts.value: About US$100 million, planned as an overwhelmingly philanthropic effort in the mold of the first Beresheet

facts.label: Funding raised
facts.value: An initial US$1 million was committed in January 2020 to start work; in July 2021 SpaceIL announced roughly US$70 million pledged by the Patrick and Lina Drahi family foundation, Morris Kahn, and the Moshal Space Foundation

facts.label: NASA cooperation
facts.value: The Israel Space Agency and NASA signed a scientific cooperation statement for the Beresheet 2 mission on 1 February 2023, covering joint science on and around the Moon

facts.label: Italy cooperation
facts.value: The Israel Space Agency and the Italian Space Agency signed a memorandum of understanding to cooperate on Beresheet 2 on 27 January 2025 at the Ilan Ramon International Space Conference in Tel Aviv; it remains a non-binding letter of intent with no funded agreement

facts.label: Donor withdrawal
facts.value: In mid-2023 the lead donors (the Drahi foundation and Morris Kahn) withdrew from further funding after roughly US$45 million had already been committed, leaving SpaceIL scrambling for alternative backing

facts.label: War impact
facts.value: SpaceIL says the fundraising crisis was worsened by the outbreak of war on 7 October 2023, which made securing large new donations far harder

facts.label: Suspension
facts.value: After a final fundraising deadline lapsed in March 2025, SpaceIL suspended engineering development in April 2025, laying off about 25 staff and consultants and freezing supplier contracts; officials call it a freeze rather than a cancellation and say a restart could enable a launch within about three years

facts.label: Predecessor
facts.value: Beresheet 2 is SpaceIL and IAI's follow-up to Beresheet, the first privately funded craft to reach lunar orbit, which crashed on Mare Serenitatis on 11 April 2019 after an IMU failure and reset command cut its main engine

timeline: Predecessor Beresheet crashes on Mare Serenitatis; SpaceIL immediately vows a second attempt
Beresheet 2 unveiled by President Rivlin as a three-craft mission (one orbiter, two landers)
About US$70 million pledged by the Drahi family foundation, Morris Kahn, and the Moshal Space Foundation
Israel Space Agency and NASA sign a science cooperation statement for Beresheet 2
Lead donors withdraw further funding after roughly US$45 million committed
Outbreak of war further complicates efforts to raise replacement funding
Israel and Italy sign a non-binding Beresheet 2 cooperation MoU at the Ramon conference
Final fundraising deadline lapses without the needed money secured
SpaceIL freezes engineering development, lays off about 25 staff and consultants, and stops short of cancelling the project

No launch target: SpaceIL said in April 2025 that a restart could lead to a launch in about three years, but there has been no restart, and SpaceIL's own site still describes engineering development as frozen for budgetary reasons (as of Oct 26, 2026)
